trails.bestSeason: Year-round (full boardwalk loop best Apr-Nov; limited winter access via guided snowcoach/ski)
trails.trailTip: Stay on the boardwalk at all times — the ground around geysers and hot springs is a thin, unstable crust over scalding water, and stepping off it causes real, severe burns most years.
trails.didYouKnow: Old Faithful is not the park's biggest geyser, but it's the most predictable, erupting every 44 to 125 minutes.

trails.trailTip: Stop at the short Grand Prismatic Overlook spur near the start — it's the best above-water view of the spring and adds only about a mile round trip.
trails.didYouKnow: At 200 feet, Fairy Falls is one of the tallest waterfalls in Yellowstone, fed by Spray and Iron Springs Creek.

trails.bestSeason: Jul-Sep (snow lingers on the upper trail into early summer)
trails.trailTip: Afternoon thunderstorms build quickly on this exposed ridge — start early and be off the summit lookout before storms roll in.
trails.didYouKnow: The fire lookout on the summit is staffed in summer and is one of the best places in the park to spot bighorn sheep along the trail.

trails.bestSeason: May-Oct (also popular in winter for wolf-watching by road)
trails.trailTip: This is prime grizzly and wolf habitat — carry bear spray, hike in a group, and use a spotting scope from a distance rather than closing in on animals in the open grassland.
trails.didYouKnow: Lamar Valley is nicknamed the 'Serengeti of North America' for the density of bison, wolves, and pronghorn visible from a single overlook.

trails.trailTip: The small trailhead parking lot at Fairy Falls fills by mid-morning in summer — arrive early or plan to walk in from an overflow area.
trails.didYouKnow: Grand Prismatic Spring's rainbow colors come from heat-loving pigmented bacteria that ring the pool, shifting color by season and water temperature.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, Storm Point is frequently closed in spring and early summer for bear activity — check current status at the Fishing Bridge Visitor Center before hiking.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail passes through a marmot colony along the lakeshore boulders before looping back through lodgepole forest.

trails.bestSeason: Jul 4-Nov 10, day use only (closed entirely Apr 1-Jul 3)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, Pelican Valley (Bear Management Area I) is closed to all entry April 1 through July 3, then open for day use only between 9 a.m. and 7 p.m. from July 4 through November 10 to protect grizzly bears — no off-trail travel or overnight camping is permitted.
trails.didYouKnow: Pelican Valley has one of the highest concentrations of grizzly bears in the lower 48 states, which is exactly why its access hours are so tightly restricted.

trails.trailTip: The trail is fully exposed to sun and wind above treeline — bring more water than you think you'll need and start early in summer.
trails.didYouKnow: Bunsen Peak is the eroded core of an ancient volcano, named after the physicist Robert Bunsen for his studies of geyser mechanics.

animals.bestSeason: Year-round (easiest to spot against snow, Nov-Mar)
animals.whereToLook: Lamar Valley and Slough Creek pullouts
animals.viewingTip: View only from established roadside pullouts using a spotting scope — stay at least 100 yards away, and never approach a den or rendezvous site, which park biologists deliberately keep unpublicized for this reason.
animals.didYouKnow: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995 after being eliminated from the park by the 1920s, and their return reshaped elk behavior and even river-bank vegetation.

animals.whereToLook: Lamar and Hayden valleys, roadside meadows
animals.viewingTip: Stay at least 25 yards away at all times and use a zoom lens for photos — bison injure more visitors than any other animal in the park, most often when people approach for a picture.
animals.didYouKnow: An adult bison can sprint up to 35 mph, three times faster than a human, despite weighing over 1,000 pounds.

animals.whereToLook: Hayden Valley and Dunraven Pass meadows
animals.viewingTip: Keep at least 100 yards away, carry bear spray, and view through binoculars or a scope rather than closing the distance — give extra space in spring when sows are out with new cubs.
animals.didYouKnow: Yellowstone grizzlies can range over hundreds of square miles and dig up whitebark pine caches and army cutworm moths as key late-summer food sources.

animals.whereToLook: Mammoth Hot Springs terraces and open valleys
animals.viewingTip: During the fall rut, bulls are aggressive and unpredictable — stay at least 25 yards back and watch from a distance with binoculars rather than approaching for a closer photo.
animals.didYouKnow: A bull elk's bugle can carry over a mile across open valleys during the September rut.

animals.whereToLook: Yellowstone River canyon rim and lake shorelines
animals.viewingTip: View nests only from established overlooks with binoculars or a scope — don't linger at the cliff edge near an active nest, since flushing a nesting adult can expose eggs or chicks to weather and predators.
animals.didYouKnow: Bald eagle nests can weigh over a ton after years of the same pair adding sticks to the same tree.

animals.viewingTip: Watch from the road with binoculars — during fawning season in late spring, fawns lie hidden and motionless in grass, so stay on established paths and don't walk through open meadows looking for them.
animals.didYouKnow: Pronghorn are the fastest land mammal in North America, capable of sustained speeds near 55 mph.

animals.whereToLook: Cliffs of the Yellowstone River canyon near Artist Point
animals.viewingTip: Scan canyon cliff ledges with binoculars from established overlooks rather than scrambling toward the rim for a closer look at a nest.
animals.didYouKnow: Ospreys dive feet-first into water to catch fish, aided by reversible outer toes that help them grip slippery prey.

animals.viewingTip: Give moose a wide berth, especially cows with calves — they can be more dangerous at close range than bears when surprised, so watch from a distance with binoculars.
animals.didYouKnow: Yellowstone's moose population has declined sharply since the 1988 fires reduced the mature willow and subalpine fir habitat they depend on.

animals.whereToLook: Quiet park lakes and slow river stretches
animals.viewingTip: Stay well back from nesting pairs on quiet ponds and rivers and view with a spotting scope from shore — approaching by foot or boat can cause a nesting pair to abandon the site.
animals.didYouKnow: Trumpeter swans are North America's heaviest native waterfowl and were once nearly extinct in the Lower 48 before protection efforts in the Yellowstone region helped them recover.
